title: Bearing capacity: how much pressure the ground can take under a footing
examples: How do you calculate the bearing capacity of soil?

explain.say: In nineteen thirteen a huge grain elevator at Transcona in Canada tilted by about twenty seven degrees within a day, as the clay beneath it gave way. It became a famous lesson in bearing capacity, the pressure the ground can carry before it fails. On the board, a two metre wide strip footing sits one metre deep in sand.

explain.say: When a footing is overloaded, a wedge of soil beneath it is pushed down as one block, shoving the soil beside it sideways and up, until the ground heaves around the footing. This is general shear failure, and the strength along those sliding surfaces sets the limit. Which soil property from the last lesson matters most here?

explain.say: Shear strength, especially the friction angle. Terzaghi turned this into a formula with three parts: cohesion, the surcharge from soil above the base, and the weight of soil under the footing. For sand with a friction angle of thirty degrees, his factors are about twenty two point five and nineteen point one.

draw.text: q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + ½ γ B N_γ

explain.say: Put in the numbers. The surcharge term is eighteen times one times twenty two point five, about four hundred and four kilopascals. The width term is half times eighteen times two times nineteen point one, about three hundred and forty four. Sand has no cohesion, so the ultimate bearing capacity is about seven hundred and forty nine kilopascals.

explain.say: We never load right to the limit. Divide by a factor of safety, usually three, to get an allowable pressure of about two hundred and fifty kilopascals, then check settlement too. Notice that a deeper base and a wider footing both raise the capacity. Great job! Challenge: what would happen to the capacity if the water table rose up to the footing base?

faq.a: Bearing capacity is the pressure a foundation can put on the ground before the soil fails in shear. The ultimate value is divided by a factor of safety to give the allowable pressure.

faq.q: What is Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation?
faq.a: For a strip footing, q u equals c N c plus gamma D f N q plus a half gamma B N gamma: a cohesion term, a surcharge term from the depth, and a width term from the soil's own weight.

faq.q: What are the bearing capacity factors?
faq.a: N c, N q and N gamma are numbers that depend only on the friction angle and grow quickly as it rises. For 30 degrees, Terzaghi's N q is about 22.5 and N gamma about 19.1.

faq.q: Why is a factor of safety of three used?
faq.a: Soil properties vary and are uncertain, and settlement often matters before failure. A factor of about 3 on ultimate bearing capacity keeps foundations safe and settlements small.
It is the classic failure of a footing on dense soil: a wedge under the footing pushes the soil sideways along clear slip surfaces, and the ground heaves up beside the footing.

facts: Karl Terzaghi set out his bearing capacity equation in Theoretical Soil Mechanics in 1943.
The Transcona grain elevator in Manitoba, Canada, tilted about 27 degrees in 1913 when the clay beneath it failed; it was later jacked back upright.
